transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been troubling you or what brings you in today?

Well, um, thank you. I just... I really didn't know where else to go because I am just so incredibly exhausted. I came in today because I’ve barely been sleeping at all. It’s been like this ever since this warehouse inspection I had to do for work. I'm an insurance underwriter, so usually, I mean, I'm just at my desk looking at policies and paperwork, but they sent me out to this commercial site, and... well, there was a blast. 

Ever since then, when I try to go to bed, I just lie there for hours. I keep replaying bits of it in my head, over and over, just staring at the ceiling and unable to stop thinking about the sequence of events. And the worst part is, on the rare occasion that I actually do manage to drift off from sheer exhaustion, it doesn't even last. I'll just suddenly jolt up, completely drenched in sweat, and I'm just wide awake. It feels exactly like I’m right back near that blast all over again. And then, of course, the whole night is ruined because there's no way I can go back to sleep after feeling like that, so I just sit there in the dark waiting for morning, which is really starting to affect my work...
How long ago was that warehouse incident, and have your sleep problems continued since then without improvement?

Well, it was... let's see, today is Thursday, so it would have been exactly a week ago yesterday. Yes, about a week. And it hasn't gotten any better at all, not even for a single night. You'd think after three or four days of getting maybe two hours of sleep a night, my body would just shut down and force me to sleep through, but it doesn't. It's like my brain is just stuck on high alert ever since that day. 

I remember the inspection was supposed to be a quick walk-through, just checking the sprinkler systems and the fire exits, you know, standard stuff. I was actually annoyed I had to go all the way out there because I had a stack of renewals on my desk. But then... well, then it happened. And literally from that very first night back in my own apartment, the sleep problems started. I thought maybe it was just the adrenaline at first, like when you drink too much coffee late in the day, but it’s been a full week now, and every single night is exactly the same routine of tossing and turning and jolting awake. I haven't had one single night of normal rest since the explosion.
Since the explosion, have you been feeling constantly on edge, easily startled, or overwhelmed by negative emotions like fear, sadness, or anger?

Oh, God, yes. Constantly on edge doesn't even begin to cover it. It's like... it's like every nerve in my body is completely frayed and exposed. I went back into the office on Monday—which, in hindsight, was probably a terrible idea, considering I haven't slept and I feel like I'm barely holding it together—but I figured I had to try and get back to normal, right? Just sit at my desk, do my underwriting, pretend everything is fine. 

But I can't. I just can't. The office is usually so quiet, you know? Just the hum of the AC and people typing. But now... every little noise feels like a physical blow. Just yesterday, the big copier down the hall jammed—it does that all the time, it makes this loud clanking noise—and I practically leaped out of my chair. My heart was pounding so hard I thought I was going to pass out. And then, later, one of the junior analysts came up behind me to ask a question about a policy rider, and he just said "Hey," and I screamed. I actually screamed in the middle of the open-plan office. I spilled my coffee everywhere. I jumped like... like the whole building was coming down around us. 

And the worst part is, it's not just a quick jump and then I'm fine. It takes me forever to calm down. I'll sit there for, I don't know, five, ten minutes, just gripping the edge of my desk, trying to catch my breath, feeling this overwhelming sense of dread, like something terrible is about to happen again. Everyone was staring at me, and I felt so embarrassed, but I couldn't stop shaking. It's just... a door slams, someone drops a book, a phone rings too loud, and my brain instantly goes right back to that warehouse, and I just panic. I've never been a jumpy person, never, but now I feel like I'm just waiting for the next disaster to strike every single second of the day.
Since the explosion, have you noticed any changes in your mood or thoughts, such as feeling hopeless, detached from others, or having trouble experiencing positive emotions?

I don't... I don't really know if I'd say I feel hopeless, exactly? It's more just... well, everything just feels so gray. Like, I don't think I'm depressed in the way people talk about being depressed, where you can't get out of bed because you're so sad, but... I just don't really feel much of anything good right now. I tried to explain it to my sister on the phone the other day. She called because we usually do this Sunday brunch thing, just the two of us, we've been doing it for years since I moved into the city. And she was going on about this new mimosa place that opened up near her apartment, and normally I'd be so excited, I love trying new places, especially with her, but I just... I couldn't even fake being interested. 

I ended up telling her I was too tired, which is true, obviously, with the sleep thing, but it was also just that the thought of sitting there, trying to smile and laugh and talk about normal things like bottomless brunch and work gossip... it just felt impossible. It felt like I was watching her talk from a million miles away. I feel really disconnected from everyone, to be honest. Even at work, before the whole screaming incident, people would be chatting by the water cooler about their weekends, and I just felt like an alien trying to study human behavior. I can't connect to what they're feeling. It's like my brain has just shut off the part that feels joy or excitement or even just normal contentment, and all that's left is this constant, exhausting hum of anxiety and exhaustion. So I wouldn't say hopeless, but definitely... definitely detached. I just feel really far away from the person I was a week ago.
Have you lost interest in activities or hobbies that you used to enjoy, or found it difficult to feel pleasure in things that would normally make you happy?

I mean, it's hard to say if I've actually lost interest, because... well, it's only been exactly a week, right? And this whole past week has really just been about trying to survive the day and get through work without having a complete breakdown in front of my coworkers. 

Normally, I'm really active. I do this indoor cycling class, like a spin class, three times a week at this boutique studio a few blocks from my apartment. The instructor, Sarah, she's absolutely great, she always plays this amazing 90s hip-hop playlist, and usually, I look forward to it all day. It's my main stress relief after dealing with insurance policies for eight hours. But this week... I haven't gone. I canceled all my classes on the app. But I don't think it's because I've lost interest in cycling, exactly? It's more like... how could I possibly sit in a dark, enclosed room with loud, pounding music and people shouting right now? Just the thought of the bass from those heavy speakers vibrating through the floor makes my chest tight. I feel like I'd have a panic attack before the warm-up was even over.

And my other big hobby is reading. I'm a huge reader, mostly historical fiction, which I usually do every single night before bed to wind down. I have this massive stack of hardcovers on my nightstand, and I was right in the middle of this really gripping novel about the Tudor court before the inspection. But since the sleep thing started, I haven't even opened a book. Not once. I'll pick it up, look at the cover, and then just put it right back down. I just lie there staring at the ceiling, or I'm too busy listening to every creak the building makes. 

So I haven't really noticed a permanent loss of interest, if that makes sense? It's not like I look at my spin shoes or my books and think, "I hate this now, I never want to do this again." It's just that right now, in this exact moment, I physically and mentally cannot bring myself to engage with any of it. I'm just too completely drained. So, yeah, I don't know if you'd count that as losing interest, or if it's just... I don't know, a temporary pause because my brain is just too full of the warehouse and the anxiety to make room for anything fun.
Since the warehouse explosion, have you found yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities that remind you of what happened?

Well, yeah, I mean... especially at work. Like I said, I went back to the office, and I'm an underwriter, so my whole job is assessing risk and reviewing these properties, right? And I handle a lot of commercial property, specifically industrial stuff. But the actual file for that warehouse... the one where the explosion happened? It's just sitting there in my digital queue. I'm supposed to be finalizing some of the paperwork on it, or at least organizing it for the claims department, but I haven't touched it. I physically can't. 

Just seeing the client's name or the property address pop up in my inbox... my stomach just completely drops. It’s this awful, heavy, sickening feeling, like I’m on a roller coaster that just went over the edge, and I literally have to click away and minimize the window before I panic. 

And the crazy thing is, it’s not even just that specific file anymore. It’s starting to bleed into everything else. Like, any calls that come in about my other industrial accounts—you know, manufacturing plants, distribution centers, anything remotely similar to that warehouse—I just sit there and stare at the caller ID on my desk phone. I let every single one of them go straight to voicemail. I know I need to answer them, I know my manager is going to pull my phone metrics at the end of the week and see that my response time is totally tanking, because usually I pride myself on clearing my queue by the end of the day. But I just... I can't do it. Even just the thought of opening an email about a standard industrial policy makes my stomach drop all over again. I'll see the subject line from a broker about a new industrial site, and I just freeze. So, I'm just avoiding all of it. I'm just letting the voicemails pile up and ignoring the emails and pretending they don't exist, which is terrible for my job, I know, but I just don't know how to force myself to look at them right now.
Have you been blaming yourself or feeling guilty about what happened during the warehouse inspection?

Guilty? No, I... I don't think so. I mean, I definitely don't blame myself for the explosion itself, because, well, I was really just there to do my job. As an underwriter, we don't always do site visits—usually, the loss control engineers handle the actual physical inspections—but my manager has been really pushing me to get more field experience this quarter so I can move up to senior underwriter next year. So I was literally just there with my hard hat and my tablet, walking a few steps behind the facility manager, checking off boxes about their fire suppression systems and verifying the square footage against the broker's application. I didn't touch any machinery, I didn't interact with whatever equipment actually caught fire. I was just observing. 

So, no, I know I didn't cause it. It was just a horrific, freak accident. A gas leak or a mechanical failure or whatever the fire marshal's official report is eventually going to say—which, like I said, I haven't read because I can't even bring myself to look at the file. But I definitely don't feel responsible for the actual event. 

If anything, I just feel... I don't know, frustrated? Unlucky? Because, honestly, I wasn't even supposed to be the one on that account in the first place. My coworker, Dan, was the lead on that specific industrial portfolio, but his wife had to be induced early—she had preeclampsia, I think, it was a whole stressful thing, but they're both fine now, thankfully—so he went on paternity leave two weeks ahead of schedule. And because he left so suddenly, his whole queue got redistributed among the rest of the team, and that specific warehouse got dumped on my desk. 

So I was the one who had to drive out to the industrial park that Tuesday. I just happened to be standing in the wrong place at the absolute wrong time. So, yeah, no guilt about causing it, and I don't think I'm blaming myself for what happened. I just... I just keep wishing I hadn't been the one assigned to go, you know? But I know it wasn't my fault. I was just doing my job.
Have you found yourself feeling unusually sad, angry, or irritable, even when you're not thinking about the warehouse incident?

I don't know if I'd say sad or angry exactly, but irritable? Absolutely. It's like my fuse is just completely gone. And it's over the stupidest, smallest things that have literally nothing to do with the warehouse or the explosion or even my industrial policies. It’s like my baseline level of patience has just evaporated. 

Like, just on Wednesday afternoon... there's this junior analyst on our team. He just started maybe three or four months ago, right out of college, and he's still learning the ropes of how we format our risk assessment spreadsheets for the senior team. And usually, I'm really patient with the new hires. I remember exactly how overwhelming it was when I first started out, so I try to be helpful. But he came over to my cubicle to ask a question about a formula—just a really simple, basic formatting thing on a spreadsheet that wasn't pulling the right data. 

And instead of just showing him how to fix it, like I normally would without a second thought, I just... I completely snapped at him. I mean, I practically bit his head off. I told him he needed to pay closer attention to the training manuals and stop wasting my time with basic questions when I'm clearly drowning in my own queue. It was way, way harsher than I meant to be. The whole row of desks got quiet, and the poor guy just looked like a deer in headlights, mumbled an apology, and practically ran back to his desk. 

And almost instantly, my face got hot and I felt so incredibly embarrassed. Because that is just not who I am. That’s not how I usually treat people, ever. I pride myself on being approachable and a good team player at work, you know? But right now, my skin just feels so thin, like every little interruption or tiny inconvenience is this massive, grating annoyance that I just can't handle. I did go over and apologize to him later by the breakroom, and I blamed it on being stressed about a deadline, but I still feel awful about it. So, yeah, the irritability is definitely there, and it's spilling over onto people who really don't deserve it at all.
Have you been feeling angry, guilty, or depressed specifically about the warehouse incident, even when you’re not directly reminded of it?

Well, like I was saying before about the guilt, I definitely don't feel guilty. And as for being depressed or angry about the actual incident... no, I really don't think I am. 

I mean, when I'm not at work, when I'm just at home in my apartment and my work laptop is physically closed and put away in my bag, I'm not sitting on my couch crying about the warehouse. I'm not, you know, fuming with rage at the universe or the facility manager or whoever's fault it ended up being. If anything, when I'm not being directly reminded of it by an email or a phone call, I'm just trying my absolute hardest to not think about it at all. I'll turn on the TV and just binge-watch some completely mindless reality show or a baking competition—something with zero stakes—just to keep my brain completely occupied with literally anything else. 

My sister actually asked me something kind of similar over the weekend. She lives out of state, but she called to check in, because she's been calling a lot since it happened, which is sweet but also kind of exhausting. Anyway, she was asking if I was feeling depressed or mourning the whole thing, and I told her the exact same thing. I'm not sad about it. I'm not walking around with this heavy, dark cloud of depression about the explosion itself. 

The irritability is definitely there, like I told you with that poor junior analyst, but that's just me being on edge in general, you know? It's my nerves being shot. It's not me being angry *about* the warehouse or the fire. So, yeah, if I don't have an industrial file staring me in the face, I'm really not feeling depressed or angry or guilty about the incident itself. I just want to zone out and pretend Tuesday never even happened.
Have you noticed that your emotional reactions, like feeling on edge or detached, have stayed about the same or gotten worse since the warehouse incident?

Well, it’s been about a week now. I mean, the inspection was last Tuesday, so yeah, it’s been exactly a week since the warehouse explosion happened. And honestly, it feels like the longest week of my entire life. I keep expecting to wake up and just feel normal again, you know? Like my nerves will finally just reset overnight after a good sleep, but they really haven't. 

I wouldn't necessarily say the feeling of being on edge has gotten worse, but it definitely hasn't gotten any better, either. It’s just stayed right at this really high, uncomfortable level for the entire week. Like, I kept thinking, okay, maybe over the weekend I'll finally decompress, or maybe starting a fresh work week on Monday would help me shake it off and get back into my normal rhythm. But then I had that whole blow-up with the junior analyst on Wednesday, which just proved that my fuse is still completely non-existent and I'm still just as tightly wound as I was the day it happened. 

So, yeah, for this whole week, ever since I was standing there at the facility when it blew up, it’s just been this constant, exhausting baseline of being totally wired. I keep waiting for the adrenaline or whatever it is to finally wear off, but it’s been seven days and my shoulders are still practically up by my ears. It’s honestly just so draining to carry this around for a whole week without any relief, just waiting to feel like myself again and having it not happen.
Even when you’re not directly reminded of the warehouse incident, do you find yourself feeling angry, guilty, or depressed about it?

I'm sorry, didn't we... I feel like we just went over this, didn't we? Or maybe my brain is just totally scattered right now, which is honestly entirely possible given how this week has gone. 

But yeah, like I was saying just a few minutes ago, I really don't have those kinds of feelings about it. I'm not depressed, I'm not guilty, and I'm not angry about the explosion itself. I know that's probably what happens in the movies, right? Someone goes through something crazy and then they spend weeks agonizing over it, weeping on the couch, or having all this deep survivor's guilt, or screaming at the universe about how unfair it all is. But I just... I don't have the energy for any of that. 

When I am not actively being forced to look at an email about the facility or deal with the fallout at work, I am doing everything in my human power to just completely blank it out. I'm just trying to exist in this little bubble where last Tuesday didn't happen. So there really isn't any room in my head to feel sad or guilty, because literally all of my mental energy is just going toward keeping it locked in a little box in the back of my mind. I just want to come home, put my keys on the counter, turn on my silly baking competitions, and completely shut down. So, no, honestly, if I'm not being reminded of it, I'm not feeling depressed or guilty at all. I'm just trying to be numb to it.

Since the warehouse incident, have you felt a loss of interest in things you used to enjoy, a sense of emotional numbness, or an inability to feel positive emotions like happiness or love, even when you're not reminded of the event?

I mean, not really? Like, I wouldn't say I've lost interest in things entirely, or that I can't feel happy at all. It's not like this big, dramatic gray filter has just dropped over my whole life where I'm suddenly a robot who can't feel joy or love or whatever. 

I was actually just telling my sister this when she called this weekend. She was asking if I was feeling, you know, detached from everything, like I couldn't enjoy my normal stuff anymore. And I told her, honestly, it's not that I don't *want* to do things I normally like. It's just that right now, my normal things—like going out with friends, or going to that spin class I usually love, or even just sitting down to read a book—they just feel like they take too much energy. And it's not because I'm depressed or numb to the world. It's just because my brain is so totally exhausted from being on high alert all the time, from just constantly humming with this nervous energy. 

So when I get home, I don't want to go out and be social, but it's not because I don't love my friends or enjoy spending time with them anymore. It's just that the idea of sitting in a loud, crowded restaurant and having to, like, perform normalcy and make conversation just sounds totally exhausting. I'd rather just sit on my couch and watch those baking shows. And I still enjoy the baking shows! I still laugh when someone drops a cake or whatever. It's not like I'm sitting there staring blankly at the screen feeling absolutely nothing. 

And as for feeling love, I mean, I still love my sister, I still love my cat—who, by the way, has been super clingy this week, it's like he knows I'm stressed. I still feel all those positive things. It's just that right now, the volume on everything else is turned down a little bit because the volume on my anxiety and my nerves is cranked up so high. But I wouldn't call it numbness, and I definitely wouldn't say I can't feel happiness. It's just... everything is just taking a backseat to this weird, wired exhaustion I'm dealing with right now.
Even when you’re not thinking about the warehouse incident, do you find yourself feeling unusually sad, guilty, or angry about it?

Wait, hold on, didn't we... I know I said my brain was scattered earlier, but I am almost entirely positive you literally just asked me this exact same question like five minutes ago. Did you? Because I feel like I'm having major déjà vu right now. 

But, I mean, my answer is still exactly the same as it was a few minutes ago. No, I don't. Like I said, I'm not sitting around feeling unusually sad, and I definitely don't feel guilty or angry about it. It’s honestly kind of frustrating to keep getting asked about being depressed or angry because it almost makes me feel like I *should* be feeling those things, you know? Like, is that the normal reaction I'm supposed to be having? Because my reaction is just this constant, buzzing anxiety. I'm not mad at the warehouse managers, I'm not feeling guilty that I was there doing my inspection when it happened, and I'm not weeping about it. 

I'm an insurance underwriter, so I look at risks and numbers all day, and maybe that makes me process things a little differently, but I really just feel completely wired, not sad. I mean, I totally understand if you have a specific clinical checklist you have to get through for your notes, because believe me, my job is basically ninety percent checklists and making sure every single box is ticked before we approve a policy, so I completely get the administrative side of having to ask things a certain way. But yeah, to answer you again, no. No unusual sadness, no guilt, no anger. Just the exhaustion and the nerves. Are there... are there a lot more questions like this that repeat? Because I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need, but I feel like I'm just saying the same thing over and over again.
Have you found it difficult to experience any positive emotions, like happiness or satisfaction, even during moments that would usually bring you joy?

Okay, I'm sorry, but I really feel like we are going in circles here. Didn't you just ask me about this, too? About not being able to feel positive emotions? I feel like I just gave a whole long explanation about this exact thing when you asked about feeling numb or not feeling love or happiness. 

But, okay, again, no. I haven't found it difficult to experience positive emotions. Like I said before, it's not that I can't feel happy or satisfied. I still feel those things. It's just that I don't have the energy to go out and seek those moments out the way I normally would. 

Like, take my job for instance. Usually, when I finish a really complicated underwriting file—you know, one of those massive commercial property ones where you have to cross-reference a dozen different risk assessments and environmental surveys—I usually feel a real sense of satisfaction when I finally hit submit and send it off for final review. It's a good feeling! Like I've solved a puzzle. And I still feel that satisfaction right now when I finish a file. It's not like I complete a huge project and just sit there feeling totally dead inside. 

The problem isn't that I can't feel the satisfaction, the problem is that just *getting* to the end of the file is taking me twice as long right now because I'm so jittery and distracted. I'm having to double-check my own math three times because my brain is just buzzing. But when I do finish it? Yes, I still feel satisfied. 

And same with happiness. Like I mentioned with the baking shows, or even just when my cat does something goofy like try to jump on the counter and miss. I still laugh. I still feel joy. It's just that those moments are happening in the middle of me feeling completely exhausted and wired. So, no, I haven't lost the ability to feel positive things. I really haven't. I'm just tired. Really, really tired. Is there... is there a reason we keep coming back to these same questions? Because I want to be helpful, I really do, but I feel like I'm just repeating myself.
Since the warehouse explosion, have you found yourself believing that the world is dangerous or that something bad is always going to happen to you?

I mean, no, not really. It’s actually kind of funny you ask that because, given my job, I literally look at worst-case scenarios all day long. Like, when I'm underwriting a commercial property policy, I have to factor in absolutely everything—fire hazards, flood zones, structural integrity, liability if someone slips on a patch of ice in the parking lot in December... I am literally paid to think about how things can go wrong and assign a numerical value to that risk. So I already know that bad things *can* happen. I'm very realistic about that. 

But I definitely don't walk around thinking the whole world is just this inherently dangerous place now, or that I'm somehow cursed and something terrible is always waiting around every corner specifically for me. The warehouse explosion... I mean, it was a freak thing. Or, well, a failure of safety protocols or equipment, which is exactly why we require those inspections in the first place before we bind a policy. But experiencing that hasn't made me think that, like, the grocery store is going to spontaneously combust while I'm buying milk, or that my apartment building is going to collapse while I'm sleeping. I'm not sitting here waiting for the sky to fall. 

It's more like... my brain is just stuck in this physical state of being on edge, like we talked about earlier. It's a physical reaction, but logically, cognitively, my mind knows I'm safe most of the time. I don't have this overarching, impending sense of doom about my life or the world. Like, I took an Uber to get to your office today, and I wasn't sitting in the back seat convinced we were going to get into a horrific, fiery crash at the next intersection. I was just a little annoyed because the driver was playing his radio way too loud and sudden noises are just making me jump right now. But I didn't think I was in actual danger, if that makes sense? I know the difference between a statistical anomaly like what happened at the warehouse and just everyday, normal life. So, no, I haven't developed this huge, pessimistic view that the world is out to get me.
Since the warehouse incident, have you had trouble remembering important parts of what happened, or found yourself having strong negative beliefs about yourself, others, or the world?

Well, like I was literally just saying about the world being dangerous, no, I don't have those strong negative beliefs. I don't blame myself, obviously, because I was just there to review their sprinkler compliance and safety logs, and I don't think everyone else is terrible or out to get me. So that part is definitely a no. 

But the memory part... that's actually something that's really been bothering me. Because usually, my memory is incredibly sharp. You kind of have to be when you're cross-referencing fifty-page building code documents and recalling specific liability clauses from memory. I pride myself on remembering details. But with the actual incident... it's like someone just took a pair of scissors and cut a scene out of a movie tape. 

I can remember exactly where I was standing right before. I was near the loading dock, looking at this disorganized stack of pallets, and I can remember hearing the explosion. It was this unbelievable, deafening boom, like it vibrated right through my chest, just this massive wall of sound. But then... I don't know. The next clear thing I have in my head is just... standing outside. I was way out by the perimeter fence in the parking lot, and I remember looking down and seeing all this black soot on my jacket. It was my favorite jacket, too, this really nice tailored beige one I wear for site visits, and it was just covered in ash. 

But how I got from the loading dock to the fence? The part in between is just blank. Completely blank. And I've tried, I mean, I have sat there in my apartment for hours trying to retrace my steps in my head, thinking, okay, did I run out the emergency exit by the breakroom? Did I follow one of the forklift drivers out? Did someone grab my arm? But no matter how hard I try to piece it together, there is just absolutely nothing there. It’s so frustrating because I like to have all the facts, I like to know exactly how things happened step-by-step, and I just... I don't have that data. It's just gone. Is that a normal thing that happens? To just lose a chunk of time like that?
Since the warehouse incident, have you experienced persistent feelings of anger, guilt, or sadness specifically related to the event, even when not directly reminded of it?

Honestly, no. Guilt doesn't even make sense in this context, if I'm being completely objective about it. I mean, why would I feel guilty? Like I mentioned earlier, my role there was strictly observational. I was just there to review their sprinkler compliance and check the safety logs before we renewed their commercial policy. It’s not like I was the facility manager or the one operating whatever machinery actually caused the spark or the pressure failure or whatever the official fire marshal report ends up saying it was. My job is to assess the risk, not manage their day-to-day operations, so I have absolutely zero personal responsibility for the fact that the explosion happened. So, no guilt at all. 

And as for anger... well, I guess you could say I was maybe a little irritated at first that my favorite tailored jacket got covered in soot, but actual, persistent anger? No. Because, again, looking at it from an underwriting perspective, catastrophic events like that are almost always the result of a cascade of small, systemic failures, right? It's rarely just one person acting maliciously. It's usually a deferred maintenance issue, or a miscommunication about safety protocols on the floor, or a faulty gauge that no one checked for six months. It's a statistical reality of industrial work. So I don't have this burning, irrational rage toward the warehouse management or anything like that. It happened, it was a failure of their systems, and that's exactly why insurance exists. 

And sadness... I mean, no, I'm not sitting at home weeping about it. I'm not walking around with this heavy cloud of depression over the event itself. I really try to keep things logical. You kind of have to in my line of work. If I got emotionally invested and started feeling profound sadness or anger over every single risk factor or liability claim I reviewed, I would literally never be able to finish a file. 

So, no, I don't really have any of those feelings. It’s not an emotional crisis for me in that way. Like I’ve been trying to explain, it’s just the physical aftermath—the buzzing in my brain, the jumping at loud noises, that weird blank spot in my memory from the loading dock to the parking lot. But emotionally? As far as anger, guilt, or sadness goes, I'm pretty detached from it. I just want my nervous system to calm down so I can do my job at my normal speed again.
Since the warehouse incident, have you had any persistent thoughts or feelings about the event that upset you emotionally, even when you weren't directly reminded of it?

I feel like this is kind of tying back into what I was just saying about the anger and sadness, so the answer is still really no. I don't have those kinds of persistent, emotionally upsetting thoughts just popping up out of nowhere. 

I mean, I'm not going to sit here and tell you the event never crosses my mind, because obviously it does, especially since I'm still trying to figure out that missing block of time from the loading dock to the parking lot that I told you about. But the way I think about it isn't emotional. It’s highly analytical. It’s like... if you're putting together a thousand-piece jigsaw puzzle and you realize you're missing a crucial edge piece. You might think about that missing piece, you might be incredibly frustrated that you can't finish the border, but you aren't sitting at the table sobbing over the puzzle or feeling this profound sense of emotional devastation. You're just annoyed by the missing data. 

That's exactly how my brain works. So if I'm just at home making dinner, or if I'm deep into reviewing a 100-page commercial property policy for a completely different client—say, a strip mall in Ohio or something—I'm not suddenly getting hit by these waves of emotional distress about the warehouse. Unless there's a loud noise that makes me physically jump, like that radio in the Uber, my mind is just focused on whatever task is right in front of me. I keep things very compartmentalized. patient.answer:
Oh, God, yes. Constantly on edge doesn't even begin to cover it. It's like... it's like every nerve in my body is completely frayed and exposed. I went back into the office on Monday—which, in hindsight, was probably a terrible idea, considering I haven't slept and I feel like I'm barely holding it together—but I figured I had to try and get back to normal, right? Just sit at my desk, do my underwriting, pretend everything is fine. 

But I can't. I just can't. The office is usually so quiet, you know? Just the hum of the AC and people typing. But now... every little noise feels like a physical blow. Just yesterday, the big copier down the hall jammed—it does that all the time, it makes this loud clanking noise—and I practically leaped out of my chair. My heart was pounding so hard I thought I was going to pass out. And then, later, one of the junior analysts came up behind me to ask a question about a policy rider, and he just said "Hey," and I screamed. I actually screamed in the middle of the open-plan office. I spilled my coffee everywhere. I jumped like... like the whole building was coming down around us. 

And the worst part is, it's not just a quick jump and then I'm fine. It takes me forever to calm down. I'll sit there for, I don't know, five, ten minutes, just gripping the edge of my desk, trying to catch my breath, feeling this overwhelming sense of dread, like something terrible is about to happen again. Everyone was staring at me, and I felt so embarrassed, but I couldn't stop shaking. It's just... a door slams, someone drops a book, a phone rings too loud, and my brain instantly goes right back to that warehouse, and I just panic. I've never been a jumpy person, never, but now I feel like I'm just waiting for the next disaster to strike every single second of the day.

Like, I don't think I'm depressed in the way people talk about being depressed, where you can't get out of bed because you're so sad, but... I just don't really feel much of anything good right now. I tried to explain it to my sister on the phone the other day. She called because we usually do this Sunday brunch thing, just the two of us, we've been doing it for years since I moved into the city. And she was going on about this new mimosa place that opened up near her apartment, and normally I'd be so excited, I love trying new places, especially with her, but I just... I couldn't even fake being interested. 

I ended up telling her I was too tired, which is true, obviously, with the sleep thing, but it was also just that the thought of sitting there, trying to smile and laugh and talk about normal things like bottomless brunch and work gossip... it just felt impossible. It felt like I was watching her talk from a million miles away. I feel really disconnected from everyone, to be honest. Even at work, before the whole screaming incident, people would be chatting by the water cooler about their weekends, and I just felt like an alien trying to study human behavior. I can't connect to what they're feeling. It's like my brain has just shut off the part that feels joy or excitement or even just normal contentment, and all that's left is this constant, exhausting hum of anxiety and exhaustion. So I wouldn't say hopeless, but definitely... definitely detached. I just feel really far away from the person I was a week ago.

Normally, I'm really active. I do this indoor cycling class, like a spin class, three times a week at this boutique studio a few blocks from my apartment. The instructor, Sarah, she's absolutely great, she always plays this amazing 90s hip-hop playlist, and usually, I look forward to it all day. It's my main stress relief after dealing with insurance policies for eight hours. But this week... I haven't gone. I canceled all my classes on the app. But I don't think it's because I've lost interest in cycling, exactly? It's more like... how could I possibly sit in a dark, enclosed room with loud, pounding music and people shouting right now? Just the thought of the bass from those heavy speakers vibrating through the floor makes my chest tight. I feel like I'd have a panic attack before the warm-up was even over.

And my other big hobby is reading. I'm a huge reader, mostly historical fiction, which I usually do every single night before bed to wind down. I have this massive stack of hardcovers on my nightstand, and I was right in the middle of this really gripping novel about the Tudor court before the inspection. But since the sleep thing started, I haven't even opened a book. Not once. I'll pick it up, look at the cover, and then just put it right back down. I just lie there staring at the ceiling, or I'm too busy listening to every creak the building makes. 

So I haven't really noticed a permanent loss of interest, if that makes sense? It's not like I look at my spin shoes or my books and think, "I hate this now, I never want to do this again." Guilty? No, I... I don't think so. I mean, I definitely don't blame myself for the explosion itself, because, well, I was really just there to do my job. As an underwriter, we don't always do site visits—usually, the loss control engineers handle the actual physical inspections—but my manager has been really pushing me to get more field experience this quarter so I can move up to senior underwriter next year. So I was literally just there with my hard hat and my tablet, walking a few steps behind the facility manager, checking off boxes about their fire suppression systems and verifying the square footage against the broker's application. I didn't touch any machinery, I didn't interact with whatever equipment actually caught fire. I was just observing. 

So, no, I know I didn't cause it. It was just a horrific, freak accident. A gas leak or a mechanical failure or whatever the fire marshal's official report is eventually going to say—which, like I said, I haven't read because I can't even bring myself to look at the file. But I definitely don't feel responsible for the actual event. 

If anything, I just feel... I don't know, frustrated? Unlucky? Because, honestly, I wasn't even supposed to be the one on that account in the first place. My coworker, Dan, was the lead on that specific industrial portfolio, but his wife had to be induced early—she had preeclampsia, I think, it was a whole stressful thing, but they're both fine now, thankfully—so he went on paternity leave two weeks ahead of schedule. And because he left so suddenly, his whole queue got redistributed among the rest of the team, and that specific warehouse got dumped on my desk. 

So I was the one who had to drive out to the industrial park that Tuesday. I just happened to be standing in the wrong place at the absolute wrong time. So, yeah, no guilt about causing it, and I don't think I'm blaming myself for what happened. I just... I just keep wishing I hadn't been the one assigned to go, you know? But I know it wasn't my fault. I was just doing my job.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient is experiencing persistent negative alterations in mood (e.g., inability to experience positive emotions) since the trauma, which would help differentiate between acute stress disorder and PTSD subtypes.
doctor.question: Have you found it difficult to experience any positive emotions, like happiness or satisfaction, even during moments that would usually bring you joy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about an inability to experience positive emotions (negative mood), which is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Okay, I'm sorry, but I really feel like we are going in circles here. Didn't you just ask me about this, too? About not being able to feel positive emotions? I feel like I just gave a whole long explanation about this exact thing when you asked about feeling numb or not feeling love or happiness. 

But, okay, again, no. I haven't found it difficult to experience positive emotions. Like I said before, it's not that I can't feel happy or satisfied. I still feel those things. It's just that I don't have the energy to go out and seek those moments out the way I normally would. 

Like, take my job for instance. Usually, when I finish a really complicated underwriting file—you know, one of those massive commercial property ones where you have to cross-reference a dozen different risk assessments and environmental surveys—I usually feel a real sense of satisfaction when I finally hit submit and send it off for final review. It's a good feeling! Like I've solved a puzzle. And I still feel that satisfaction right now when I finish a file. It's not like I complete a huge project and just sit there feeling totally dead inside. 

The problem isn't that I can't feel the satisfaction, the problem is that just *getting* to the end of the file is taking me twice as long right now because I'm so jittery and distracted. I'm having to double-check my own math three times because my brain is just buzzing. But when I do finish it? Yes, I still feel satisfied. 

And same with happiness. Like I mentioned with the baking shows, or even just when my cat does something goofy like try to jump on the counter and miss. I still laugh. I still feel joy. It's just that those moments are happening in the middle of me feeling completely exhausted and wired. So, no, I haven't lost the ability to feel positive things. I really haven't. I'm just tired. Really, really tired. Is there... is there a reason we keep coming back to these same questions? Because I want to be helpful, I really do, but I feel like I'm just repeating myself.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent negative emotional state related to the trauma, specifically persistent negative beliefs about oneself, others, or the world.
doctor.question: Since the warehouse explosion, have you found yourself believing that the world is dangerous or that something bad is always going to happen to you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about persistent negative beliefs or expectations about the world or oneself, which is not covered by any of my symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I mean, no, not really. It’s actually kind of funny you ask that because, given my job, I literally look at worst-case scenarios all day long. Like, when I'm underwriting a commercial property policy, I have to factor in absolutely everything—fire hazards, flood zones, structural integrity, liability if someone slips on a patch of ice in the parking lot in December... I am literally paid to think about how things can go wrong and assign a numerical value to that risk. So I already know that bad things *can* happen. I'm very realistic about that. 

But I definitely don't walk around thinking the whole world is just this inherently dangerous place now, or that I'm somehow cursed and something terrible is always waiting around every corner specifically for me. The warehouse explosion... I mean, it was a freak thing. Or, well, a failure of safety protocols or equipment, which is exactly why we require those inspections in the first place before we bind a policy. But experiencing that hasn't made me think that, like, the grocery store is going to spontaneously combust while I'm buying milk, or that my apartment building is going to collapse while I'm sleeping. I'm not sitting here waiting for the sky to fall. 

It's more like... my brain is just stuck in this physical state of being on edge, like we talked about earlier. It's a physical reaction, but logically, cognitively, my mind knows I'm safe most of the time. I don't have this overarching, impending sense of doom about my life or the world. Like, I took an Uber to get to your office today, and I wasn't sitting in the back seat convinced we were going to get into a horrific, fiery crash at the next intersection. I was just a little annoyed because the driver was playing his radio way too loud and sudden noises are just making me jump right now. But I didn't think I was in actual danger, if that makes sense? I know the difference between a statistical anomaly like what happened at the warehouse and just everyday, normal life. So, no, I haven't developed this huge, pessimistic view that the world is out to get me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient is experiencing persistent negative alterations in mood or cognition related to the trauma, which would help distinguish between acute stress disorder and PTSD subtypes.
doctor.question: Since the warehouse incident, have you had trouble remembering important parts of what happened, or found yourself having strong negative beliefs about yourself, others, or the world?

target_item.name: Trauma_Related_Amnesia
target_item.manifestation: I can remember hearing the explosion and I can remember standing outside afterward with soot on my jacket, but the part in between is just blank no matter how hard I try to piece it together.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question specifically asks about having trouble remembering important parts of what happened during the incident, which aligns with Trauma-Related Amnesia.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was literally just saying about the world being dangerous, no, I don't have those strong negative beliefs. I don't blame myself, obviously, because I was just there to review their sprinkler compliance and safety logs, and I don't think everyone else is terrible or out to get me. So that part is definitely a no. 

But the memory part... that's actually something that's really been bothering me. Because usually, my memory is incredibly sharp. You kind of have to be when you're cross-referencing fifty-page building code documents and recalling specific liability clauses from memory. I pride myself on remembering details. But with the actual incident... it's like someone just took a pair of scissors and cut a scene out of a movie tape. 

I can remember exactly where I was standing right before. I was near the loading dock, looking at this disorganized stack of pallets, and I can remember hearing the explosion. It was this unbelievable, deafening boom, like it vibrated right through my chest, just this massive wall of sound. But then... I don't know. The next clear thing I have in my head is just... standing outside. I was way out by the perimeter fence in the parking lot, and I remember looking down and seeing all this black soot on my jacket. It was my favorite jacket, too, this really nice tailored beige one I wear for site visits, and it was just covered in ash. 

But how I got from the loading dock to the fence? The part in between is just blank. Completely blank. And I've tried, I mean, I have sat there in my apartment for hours trying to retrace my steps in my head, thinking, okay, did I run out the emergency exit by the breakroom? Did I follow one of the forklift drivers out? Did someone grab my arm? But no matter how hard I try to piece it together, there is just absolutely nothing there. It’s so frustrating because I like to have all the facts, I like to know exactly how things happened step-by-step, and I just... I don't have that data. It's just gone. Is that a normal thing that happens? To just lose a chunk of time like that?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient is experiencing persistent negative emotional state (e.g., anger, guilt, sadness) specifically related to the trauma, which would help differentiate between acute stress disorder and PTSD subtypes
doctor.question: Since the warehouse incident, have you experienced persistent feelings of anger, guilt, or sadness specifically related to the event, even when not directly reminded of it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about persistent negative emotional states (such as anger, guilt, or sadness related to the event), which corresponds to a different symptom criterion. The patient's profile includes 'Irritability_Aggression' (S077), but that refers to irritable behavior and angry outbursts, not persistent internal feelings of guilt or sadness.

patient.answer:
Honestly, no. Guilt doesn't even make sense in this context, if I'm being completely objective about it. I mean, why would I feel guilty? Like I mentioned earlier, my role there was strictly observational. I was just there to review their sprinkler compliance and check the safety logs before we renewed their commercial policy. It’s not like I was the facility manager or the one operating whatever machinery actually caused the spark or the pressure failure or whatever the official fire marshal report ends up saying it was. My job is to assess the risk, not manage their day-to-day operations, so I have absolutely zero personal responsibility for the fact that the explosion happened. So, no guilt at all. 

And as for anger... well, I guess you could say I was maybe a little irritated at first that my favorite tailored jacket got covered in soot, but actual, persistent anger? No. Because, again, looking at it from an underwriting perspective, catastrophic events like that are almost always the result of a cascade of small, systemic failures, right? It's rarely just one person acting maliciously. It's usually a deferred maintenance issue, or a miscommunication about safety protocols on the floor, or a faulty gauge that no one checked for six months. It's a statistical reality of industrial work. So I don't have this burning, irrational rage toward the warehouse management or anything like that. It happened, it was a failure of their systems, and that's exactly why insurance exists. 

And sadness... I mean, no, I'm not sitting at home weeping about it. I'm not walking around with this heavy cloud of depression over the event itself. I really try to keep things logical. You kind of have to in my line of work. If I got emotionally invested and started feeling profound sadness or anger over every single risk factor or liability claim I reviewed, I would literally never be able to finish a file. 

So, no, I don't really have any of those feelings. It’s not an emotional crisis for me in that way. Like I’ve been trying to explain, it’s just the physical aftermath—the buzzing in my brain, the jumping at loud noises, that weird blank spot in my memory from the loading dock to the parking lot. But emotionally? As far as anger, guilt, or sadness goes, I'm pretty detached from it. I just want my nervous system to calm down so I can do my job at my normal speed again.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent negative emotional state (e.g., anger, guilt, sadness) specifically tied to the event, which would support a more complex PTSD presentation (F43.11 or F43.12) rather than acute stress disorder (F43.10).
doctor.question: Since the warehouse incident, have you had any persistent thoughts or feelings about the event that upset you emotionally, even when you weren't directly reminded of it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about persistent negative emotional states or persistent upsetting thoughts/feelings related to the event, which is not covered by any of my symptom profiles (and I just denied anger, guilt, and sadness).

patient.answer:
I feel like this is kind of tying back into what I was just saying about the anger and sadness, so the answer is still really no. I don't have those kinds of persistent, emotionally upsetting thoughts just popping up out of nowhere. 

I mean, I'm not going to sit here and tell you the event never crosses my mind, because obviously it does, especially since I'm still trying to figure out that missing block of time from the loading dock to the parking lot that I told you about. But the way I think about it isn't emotional. It’s highly analytical. It’s like... if you're putting together a thousand-piece jigsaw puzzle and you realize you're missing a crucial edge piece. You might think about that missing piece, you might be incredibly frustrated that you can't finish the border, but you aren't sitting at the table sobbing over the puzzle or feeling this profound sense of emotional devastation. You're just annoyed by the missing data. 

That's exactly how my brain works. So if I'm just at home making dinner, or if I'm deep into reviewing a 100-page commercial property policy for a completely different client—say, a strip mall in Ohio or something—I'm not suddenly getting hit by these waves of emotional distress about the warehouse. Unless there's a loud noise that makes me physically jump, like that radio in the Uber, my mind is just focused on whatever task is right in front of me. I keep things very compartmentalized. I've spent years training my brain to look at disasters objectively, assigning numerical risk values to worst-case scenarios, so I don't really have the bandwidth to just sit around and be emotionally tormented by thoughts of the explosion when nothing is even reminding me of it. It just wouldn't be productive, you know? I really just try to stick to the facts.
